verses.zh: 神有治理之权，有威严可畏；他在高处施行和平。
verses.en: “Dominion[NOTE:1] and awesome might[NOTE:2] belong to[NOTE:3] God;he establishes peace in his heights.[NOTE:4]
notes: The third speech of Bildad takes up Job 25, a short section of six verses. It is followed by two speeches from Job; and Zophar does not return with his third. Does this mean that the friends have run out of arguments, and that Job is just getting going? Many scholars note that in chs. 26 and 27 there is material that does not fit Job’s argument. Many have rearranged the material to show that there was a complete cycle of three speeches. In that light, 26:5-14 is viewed as part of Bildad’s speech. Some, however, take Bildad’s speech to be only ch. 25, and make 26:5-14 an interpolated hymn. For all the arguments and suggestions, one should see the introductions and the commentaries.
The word הַמְשֵׁל (hamshel) is a Hiphil infinitive absolute used as a noun. It describes the rulership or dominion that God has, that which gives power and authority.
The word פָּחַד (pakhad) literally means “fear; dread,” but in the sense of what causes the fear or the dread.
verses.commentary:
25:2-3 This is a series of descriptive phrases of who God is (i.e., His attributes).

- dominion (BDB 605, KB 647, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE. This
is a royal affirmation (cf. Ps. 8:6). God is king. The rabbis address Deity as "the
King of the Universe."

- awe (BDB 808 I), which denotes an appropriate respect for Deity (cf. Job 13:11; 23:15;
Ps. 14:5; 36:1; 119:120). It is often translated "fear" or "dread."

- establishes peace (between angels, cf. Isa. 24:21) in His heights (BDB 928), which
refers to God's dwelling place in the heights (cf. Job 31:2). This could refer to

- a high mountain (i.e., Mt. Seir, Mt. Sinai, mountain in the far north; cf. Ezek. 20:40)

- in highest heaven (cf. Isa. 57:15, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN and the Third Heaven)

- highest rank

- captain of the innumerable armies (angels) of God (i.e., God as Lord Saboath,
Lord of Hosts, cf. Jos. 5:13-15)a

- God of creation (i.e., light) or revelation (i.e., light). The NJB sees this as reference
to "lightning" as a metaphorical weapon of God

Light (BDB 21) has several connotations in the OT.

- special provision by God during the exodus and wilderness wandering period
to express His presence, care, protection, and guidance (cf. Exod. 10:23; 13:21-22; 14:20; Ps. 78:14)

- metaphor of revealing truth (cf. Ezra 9:8; Ps. 112:4; Job 28:11; expressed negatively in Job 12:25;
also note Job 5:14)

- special revelation of His will (cf. Job 29:3; Ps. 43:3; 119:105; Prov. 6:23; Isa. 42:6; 49:6; 51:4)

- imagery for God Himself (cf. Job 22:28; 24:13; 33:28; Ps. 27:1; 90:8; Isa. 10:17; 60:1-2,19-20)

There is an obvious semantic overlap in these verses.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

25:3a There are several places in
the Bible that speak about a large number of angels (cf. Deut. 33:2; 2
Kgs. 6:17; Ps. 68:17; Dan. 7:10; Matt. 26:53; Heb. 12:22; Rev. 5:11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS

verses.zh: 他的诸军岂能数算？他的光亮一发，谁不蒙照呢？
verses.en: Can his armies be numbered?[NOTE:1] On whom does his light[NOTE:2] not rise?
notes: The line says that God “makes peace in his heights.” The “heights” are usually interpreted to mean the highest heaven. There may be a reference here to combat in the spiritual world between angels and Satan. The context will show that God has a heavenly host at his disposal, and nothing in heaven or on earth can shatter his peace. “Peace” here could also signify the whole order he establishes.
Heb “Is there a number to his troops?” The question is rhetorical: there is no number to them!

verses.zh: 这样在　神面前，人怎能称义？妇人所生的怎能洁净？
verses.en: How then can a human being be righteous before God?How can one born of a woman be pure?[NOTE:1]
notes: In place of “light” here the LXX has “his ambush,” perhaps reading אֹרְבוֹ (ʾorevo) instead of אוֹרֵהוּ (ʾorehu, “his light”). But while that captures the idea of troops and warfare, the change should be rejected because the armies are linked with stars and light. The expression is poetic; the LXX interpretation tried to make it concrete.
verses.commentary:
25:4 This is a crucial
theological question in Job (cf. Job 4:17; 15:14). It addresses the
condition of fallen humanity (see litany of OT texts in Rom. 3:10-18;
and summary in Rom. 3:23 and Gal. 3:22). How can Job claim to be innocent?
Eliphaz also asserts the sinfulness of all humans in Job 4:17-19.
However, Job claims that his youthful sins were not so great as to
deserve the awful judgments of Job 1-2. His three comforters' commitment
to "the two ways" demands Job's sinfulness in order to
maintain their theological worldview.

verses.zh: 在　神眼前，月亮也无光亮，星宿也不清洁。
verses.en: If even the moon is not bright,and the stars are not pure as far as he is concerned,[NOTE:1]
notes: Bildad here does not come up with new expressions; rather, he simply uses what Eliphaz had said (see Job 4:17-19 and 15:14-16).
verses.commentary:
25:5 Both Eliphaz (Job 4:18;
15:15) and Bildad assert that the fall of mankind (i.e., Genesis 3) has
affected the heavens (i.e., even angels are not completely pure). I am
assuming the creation imagery of Job 25:5 refers to angels. In the ANE,
particularly Babylon, the lights of the day and night sky were viewed as
spiritual beings (cf. Isa. 40:26).

verses.zh: 何况如虫的人，如蛆的世人呢！
verses.en: how much less a mortal man, who is but a maggot[NOTE:1]—a son of man, who is only a worm!”
verses.commentary:
25:6 "maggot. . .worm" These are in a synonymous parallel relationship
(as are "man" and "son of man"). Both of these are hyperboles for

- frailty (disease) of mankind, cf. Job 7:5; Isa. 41:14

- death of mankind, cf. Job 17:14; 21:26; 24:20; Isa. 14:11

- rottenness of mankind (KB 1241, #1), cf. Exod. 16:24; in this context this connotation fits best

- insignificance of a worm in Ps. 22:6

In one sense Bildad is correct about the corruption of humanity, but
this is only the result of the rebellion of Genesis 3 (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND). Originally mankind was

- personally created by God (Gen. 2:7)

- created in the image and likeness of God Himself (Gen. 1:26-27)

- created for fellowship with God (Gen. 3:8) in a special place created for them
(i.e., the Garden of Eden)

- God plans for the restoration of fellowship damaged in Gen. 3:1-7. This is
clearly seen in Gen. 3:15

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "the son of man"
This is simply a Hebrew idiom for humanity (cf. Job 7:17; Ps. 8:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SON OF MAN

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why is Bildad's speech so short? Along the same lines, why is there no speech of Zophar recorded?

- Does Job 25:2b refer to conflict in heaven among angels?

- To what does "His light" refer?

- Why is Job 25:4 such an important verse? Is Bildad referring directly to Job's claim of innocence?

- Does Job 25:5 refer to impurity or rebellion among the angels?

- Explain Job 25:6 in your own words.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This third cycle of speeches is incomplete and truncated. There
have been many suggestions on textual rearrangement and the assigning of
certain passages to the comforter whose section is short (Bildad) or
missing (Zophar). Also notice the unusually long length of Job's
response (i.e., Job 26-31). See chart of the dialogues in Contextual Insights, chapter 20.

- The theme of the evil of mankind has been addressed several times.

- Eliphaz – Job 4:17-21; 15:14-16

- Zophar – Job 11:5-12

- Job – Job 9:2-12; 14:4

- In context this brief chapter is another attempt by the three comforters
to address Job's claim of innocence.

- It is possible that UBS Handbook (p. 464), TEV, and NJB are correct in seeing

- Bildad's speech going from Job 25:1-6 and continuing at 26:5-14

- this would make Job 26:1-4 a brief response from Job (or as the Jewish Study
Bible says, a part of Bildad's speech)

- my problem with all of the textual division and rearrangement is

- there is not agreement among scholars

- the cosmological passage of Job 26:5-14 is artistic and powerful
poetry, which does not fit the other speeches of Bildad
